Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: GI Cancer Epidemiology & Risk Factors
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
"GI" is several very different cancers along one tube. Each has its own typical patient, causes, and prognosis. Recognizing the patterns is what lets you connect "trouble swallowing," "blood in the stool," or "painless jaundice" to the right diagnosis. Radiation matters most for the esophagus, rectum, anus, and pancreas, with growing roles in the liver and a smaller one in the stomach.

The Big Picture

SiteHow common / deadlyMain driversHistology
EsophagusLifetime risk ~0.5%; usually found lateSCC: smoking, alcohol. Adeno: GERD, Barrett's, obesitySCC (worldwide) / adenocarcinoma (US)
StomachCommon worldwide (East Asia), less in the USH. pylori, smoked/salted foods, CDH1 (diffuse type)Adenocarcinoma
Pancreas3rd–4th leading cause of cancer death; ~13% 5-year survivalSmoking, diabetes, obesity, chronic pancreatitis, BRCA/LynchDuctal adenocarcinoma
Liver (HCC)Rising in the USCirrhosis: hepatitis B/C, alcohol, fatty liverHepatocellular carcinoma
Rectum~40% of colorectal cancer (colorectal = #3 cancer and #2–3 cause of cancer death)Age, diet, IBD, Lynch, FAP; rising in young adultsAdenocarcinoma
Anal canalRare (rectal is ~5× more common); highly curableHPV, HIV, smoking, immunosuppressionSquamous cell carcinoma
Rectal = adenocarcinoma, surgery-centered. Anal = HPV squamous cell, chemoradiation-centered. Neighbors, but different diseases.

Esophageal Cancer

Presents in the 60s–70s with progressive dysphagia (solids, then liquids) and weight loss. Two histologies behave like two diseases sharing one organ:

Squamous cell (SCC)
Upper/mid esophagus

~90% worldwide. Mnemonic "ABCDEF": Achalasia/alcohol, Bad diet (hot liquids, nitrosamines), Caustic stricture/cigarettes, Diverticula, Esophageal webs (Plummer-Vinson), Familial (tylosis). More radiosensitive.

Adenocarcinoma (ACA)
Distal esophagus / GEJ

~70% in the US. Mnemonic "BOG": Barrett's, Obesity, GERD (weekly symptoms ~5× risk, daily ~7×). Also male sex, white race.

Stomach and Liver (Briefly)

  • Gastric cancer: H. pylori (intestinal type), smoked/salted foods, smoking, pernicious anemia; CDH1 mutation causes hereditary diffuse gastric cancer. Signs: early satiety, weight loss, anemia. Surgery + perioperative chemo is the core; RT has a limited role.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma: nearly always on a background of cirrhosis (hepatitis B can cause HCC without it). Cirrhotic patients get ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months. Liver function (Child-Pugh) often limits treatment as much as the tumor does.

Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma

Only the ~11th most common cancer, but one of the top causes of cancer death, because it's usually found late. About half present with metastases. Five-year survival: ~44% localized, ~16% regional, ~3% distant.

1
Modifiable

Smoking (the biggest), obesity, heavy alcohol, chronic pancreatitis, long-standing diabetes, red meat.

2
Hereditary

BRCA1/2, PALB2, Lynch, Peutz-Jeghers (STK11), FAMMM (CDKN2A), hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1). High-risk people get EUS/MRI screening.

3
Presentation

Painless jaundice (head), back pain and weight loss (body/tail), new-onset diabetes, Trousseau sign (migratory thrombophlebitis).

Clinical Pearl

New-onset diabetes plus unexplained weight loss in someone over 50 should raise suspicion for pancreatic cancer.

Rectal Cancer

  • Colorectal cancer lifetime risk ~4%; rectal cancer is ~40% of it. Incidence is rising in adults under 50, so average-risk screening now starts at 45 (colonoscopy every 10 years is the gold standard).
  • Presentation: bright red blood per rectum, change in bowel habits, tenesmus, iron-deficiency anemia.
  • Risk factors: age, family history, IBD, obesity, red/processed meat, smoking, alcohol, prior pelvic RT.
SyndromeGeneKey features
Lynch (HNPCC)MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 (mismatch repair)MSI-high tumors; also endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urinary tract cancers; colonoscopy from 20–25. MMR-deficient tumors respond to immunotherapy.
FAPAPCHundreds to thousands of polyps; prophylactic colectomy. Gardner (osteomas, desmoids), Turcot (brain tumors)

Anal Cancer

  • Rare (lifetime risk ~1 in 500), average age ~60s, about twice as common in women.
  • HPV in 85–90% (mostly HPV-16). Highest risk: people with HIV, other immunosuppression, smoking, receptive anal intercourse, prior cervical/vulvar/vaginal cancer or dysplasia.
  • Presentation: bleeding, pain, a mass, itching. Often misattributed to hemorrhoids.
  • Usually local or locoregional at diagnosis, and highly curable with chemoradiation.
Clinical Pearl

Don't confuse anal and rectal cancer. Anal cancer is HPV-driven squamous cell carcinoma treated with definitive chemoRT (surgery for salvage). Rectal cancer is adenocarcinoma, where surgery is the central curative step.

Self-check: a 48-year-old with HIV has rectal bleeding blamed on hemorrhoids for a year. What should you worry about?▾

Anal cancer. HIV is a major risk factor; bleeding and pain are often dismissed as hemorrhoids. Exam, anoscopy, and biopsy of any mass.

High-Yield Summary
  • Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is in the upper or mid esophagus and linked to smoking and alcohol, while adenocarcinoma is distal or at the GEJ and linked to Barrett's, obesity, and GERD.
  • Pancreatic cancer classically presents with painless jaundice or new diabetes with weight loss, and smoking is the main modifiable risk factor.
  • Rectal cancer is an adenocarcinoma with surgery as the backbone of treatment, and Lynch syndrome (MSI-high) tumors respond to immunotherapy.
  • Anal cancer is a squamous cancer driven by HPV, with higher risk in HIV, and chemoradiation cures most patients without surgery.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma arises in cirrhotic livers (hepatitis B or C, alcohol, fatty liver), so patients with cirrhosis are screened every 6 months.

Anatomy & Lymphatics.title: The GI Tract: Anatomy, Levels & Lymph Nodes
Anatomy & Lymphatics.html:
GI anatomy is a trip down one long tube. At every stop you need three things: the organ's regions (which set the stage and the surgery), what's next to it (the organs at risk), and where it drains (which nodes go in the field). This page has two interactive modules: the organs from top to bottom and the nodal basins for each site. The axial CT levels are in the Imaging module.

The GI Tract, Top to Bottom

Esophagus: Location by Distance

SegmentDistance from incisorsNotes
Cervical15–20 cmCricopharyngeus to the thoracic inlet; treated like head and neck (definitive chemoRT)
Upper thoracic20–25 cmBehind the trachea; carina at ~25 cm
Middle thoracic25–30 cmBehind the left atrium
Lower thoracic30–40 cmBarrett's and adenocarcinoma
GEJ~40 cmSiewert I–II treated as esophageal; III as gastric
  • The esophagus has no serosa, so tumors spread into the mediastinum early.
  • A longitudinal submucosal lymphatic network lets tumor spread several cm up and down: RT margins are ~3–4 cm longitudinally but ~1 cm radially.

Pancreas and Liver

  • Pancreas: head (with the uncinate process, ~70% of cancers, painless jaundice), neck (over the SMV/portal vein), body, tail (near the spleen).
  • Resectability depends on vessels: arteries (SMA, celiac, common hepatic) and veins (SMV, portal vein). Details in Workup & Staging.
  • Liver: 8 Couinaud segments; the portal vein brings 75% of blood (HCC is fed by the hepatic artery, which is why it enhances early). The dome moves several cm with breathing.

Rectum and Anal Canal

Rectum
Measured from the anal verge
  • Low 0–5 cm, mid 5–10, upper 10–15 cm
  • Wrapped in the mesorectum, bounded by the mesorectal fascia (MRF)
  • TME removes the mesorectum intact; the MRF is the surgical margin
  • Upper rectum above the peritoneal reflection behaves more like colon
Anal canal
~3–4 cm long
  • From the anorectal ring (top of the puborectalis) to the anal verge
  • Dentate line splits the drainage: above → mesorectal/internal iliac, below → inguinal
  • Internal and external sphincters (continence)
  • Anal margin: the skin within 5 cm of the verge
Self-check: a rectal tumor's lower edge is 3 cm from the anal verge. Why does that height matter so much?▾

It's a low rectal cancer: surgery may need an APR (permanent colostomy), the mesorectum is thin (margins are harder), and it's the prime case for total neoadjuvant therapy aiming for organ preservation (watch-and-wait).

The Lymph Nodes: Drainage by Organ

SiteRegional nodes (in the field)Distant (M1)
EsophagusPeriesophageal nodes from the neck to the celiac (paratracheal, subcarinal, paraesophageal, left gastric, celiac)Supraclavicular and beyond
StomachPerigastric, left gastric, common hepatic, splenic, celiacPara-aortic, retropancreatic (beyond D2)
PancreasPeripancreatic, hepatic artery, celiac, SMAPara-aortic
RectumMesorectal, superior rectal/IMA, internal iliac, obturator, presacralExternal iliac, inguinal (unless the tumor invades the anal canal or an anterior organ)
Anal canalInguinal, mesorectal, internal iliac, external iliac, presacralCommon iliac and above
Rectum: pelvic nodes only; groins are distant. Anus: groins are always regional and always in the field.
  • N stage counts nodes for most GI sites: esophagus N1 1–2, N2 3–6, N3 ≥7; colorectal N1 1–3, N2 ≥4; pancreas N1 1–3, N2 ≥4. Anal cancer uses location instead (N1a inguinal/mesorectal/internal iliac, N1b external iliac, N1c both).
  • Rectal CTV: the tumor, the whole mesorectum, presacral, internal iliac, and obturator nodes; add external iliac for T4 into anterior organs and inguinal if the anal canal is involved.
High-Yield Summary
  • The esophagus is described by distance from the incisors, with the GEJ at about 40 cm, and because it has no serosa and spreads along its length, RT fields use long margins.
  • Rectal tumors are called low, mid, or upper by distance from the anal verge, and the mesorectal fascia is the surgical (TME) plane.
  • The dentate line splits anal drainage, so tumors below it drain to the inguinal nodes.
  • Inguinal and external iliac nodes are regional for anal cancer but distant (M1) for rectal cancer.
  • Pancreatic resectability depends on the SMA, celiac axis, common hepatic artery, and SMV/portal vein, so learn where each one sits.

Imaging.title: GI Imaging: MRI, CT, EUS & PET/CT
Imaging.html:
Each primary is grouped below, from the esophagus down to the anus, with its normal axial anatomy first and then its key staging scan. In short: MRI for the rectum and liver, pancreatic-protocol CT for the pancreas, EUS + PET/CT for the esophagus, and PET/CT for anal cancer. The planning CT (with 4D-CT for upper abdominal targets) is where it all comes together. This section comes before Workup & Staging because staging these cancers is mostly reading these studies.

SiteKey local studyDistant staging
EsophagusEUS (T and nodes), endoscopy (length, distance)PET/CT
StomachEUS, CT; diagnostic laparoscopy (peritoneal disease)CT ± PET
PancreasPancreatic-protocol CT (or MRI)CT chest; MRI liver if unclear
Liver (HCC)Multiphase MRI or CT (LI-RADS)CT chest
RectumHigh-resolution pelvic MRICT chest/abdomen/pelvis
AnusPelvic MRI, examPET/CT

Esophagus

  • EUS sees the wall layers: T1a (mucosa) can be removed endoscopically; T1b (submucosa) and deeper need surgery or chemoRT.
  • PET/CT finds nodes and distant disease (changes management in ~15–20%) and helps define the tumor length for contouring.
  • Upper/mid tumors near the airway: bronchoscopy to rule out tracheal invasion or fistula.
  • Planning: 4D-CT for distal tumors (they move with breathing); CTV = GTV + ~3–4 cm up and down, ~1 cm radially (CROSS used 4 cm longitudinally).
  • On the normal levels: the upper thoracic esophagus sits behind the trachea at the aortic arch; the mid esophagus sits right behind the left atrium, next to the subcarinal nodes.
  • Organs at risk at this level: spinal cord, lungs, trachea, and the heart (mid and distal tumors).

Stomach and GEJ

  • EUS is preferred when early-stage disease is suspected; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for everyone, and PET/CT for locally advanced disease.
  • CT misses peritoneal disease, so diagnostic laparoscopy with washings is done before curative surgery (positive cytology = M1).
  • The GEJ and stomach move with breathing: plan with 4D-CT.
  • Organs at risk at this level: liver, stomach, spleen, kidneys, and heart.

Pancreas

  • Thin-slice CT in arterial (pancreatic) and portal venous phases. The tumor is hypoenhancing (dark).
  • Double duct sign: dilated common bile duct + pancreatic duct = pancreatic head (or ampullary) mass.
  • Describe each vessel: degrees of contact (≤180° vs >180°) with the SMA, celiac, CHA, and SMV/PV, and any vein contour irregularity.
  • Get the scan before a biliary stent if possible (stents cause inflammation that blurs the edges).
  • CA 19-9 is followed, but it's falsely high with jaundice and absent in Lewis-antigen-negative patients.
  • Organs at risk at this level: duodenum, stomach, kidneys, liver, and spinal cord.

Liver (HCC)

  • Arterial hyperenhancement + washout + capsule in a cirrhotic liver = LI-RADS 5: HCC can be diagnosed without a biopsy.
  • Portal vein tumor thrombus is common and can be treated with SBRT.
  • For SBRT: 4D-CT or breath hold (the liver moves 1–3 cm), fiducials for daily alignment, and contrast-enhanced planning.

Rectum

Rectal MRI answers the questions that decide who needs neoadjuvant therapy:

1
T stage

Intact dark muscularis propria = T1–2. Into mesorectal fat = T3 (a–d by depth). Peritoneum or other organs = T4.

2
MRF

Tumor, node, or EMVI ≤1 mm from the mesorectal fascia = threatened CRM: the strongest predictor of local recurrence.

3
EMVI

Tumor in extramural veins: predicts distant metastases. Pushes toward TNT.

4
Nodes & height

Mesorectal and lateral nodes (by border and signal, not just size); distance from the anal verge and sphincter involvement.

  • A restaging MRI after neoadjuvant therapy (with endoscopy) decides whether the patient has a complete clinical response and can try watch-and-wait. Look for dark fibrosis without residual intermediate-signal tumor or restricted diffusion.
  • Organs at risk at this level: bladder, small bowel, and femoral heads.

Anus

  • PET/CT finds inguinal and pelvic nodes that CT misses, upstaging ~20% and changing the RT dose to involved nodes.
  • Pelvic MRI defines local extent (sphincters, vagina, prostate).
  • Response imaging after chemoRT: wait (tumors keep shrinking for months; judge at up to 26 weeks).
  • On CT, the inguinal nodes sit along the femoral vessels in the groin and are always in the elective field.
  • Organs at risk at this level: genitalia, femoral heads, bladder, and perineal skin.
Self-check: rectal MRI shows a T3 tumor with a mesorectal node 0.8 mm from the mesorectal fascia. Is the margin threatened?▾

Yes. A tumor, node, tumor deposit, or EMVI within 1 mm of the MRF all count as a threatened margin. This patient needs neoadjuvant therapy (usually TNT with long-course chemoRT).

High-Yield Summary
  • Rectal MRI is the key staging test because it shows T stage, the distance to the mesorectal fascia (1 mm or less is threatened), EMVI, and involved nodes.
  • Pancreatic-protocol CT shows the mass and how much it touches the major vessels, which decides resectability.
  • Esophageal cancer is staged with EUS for depth of invasion and PET/CT for nodes and metastases.
  • Anal cancer response is judged up to 26 weeks after chemoradiation, because tumors keep shrinking for months.
  • HCC can be diagnosed on multiphase CT or MRI without a biopsy when it shows arterial enhancement with washout (LI-RADS 5).

Workup & Staging.title: GI Cancer Workup & Staging
Workup & Staging.html:
GI cancers are staged with the AJCC TNM system, but at the point of care each site really turns on only one or two features. Learn the pattern first, then the exceptions. The NCCN workup and full AJCC tables are at the bottom of the page.

The One Pattern That Repeats

Across almost every GI site, the same three questions build the stage:

T
How deep through the wall?

The GI wall layers are the same everywhere: mucosa → submucosa → muscularis propria → beyond the wall (adventitia/serosa/fat) → adjacent organs. Deeper = higher T.

N
How many regional nodes?

Most GI sites count nodes (1–2 vs 3–6 vs ≥7 is the recurring esophagus/stomach rhythm). Anus is the exception: it uses node location, not number.

M
Distant spread?

Includes non-regional nodes and, for stomach, pancreas, and the esophagogastric junction, positive peritoneal cytology even with no visible implants.

The Two Sites That Break the Pattern

Memorize these as exceptions:

Pancreas
Staged by resectability

Not staged by TNM in practice. It's staged by resectability: tumor contact with arteries and veins on pancreatic-protocol CT.

Liver (HCC)
Staged by BCLC

BCLC blends tumor burden + liver function + performance status, because the cirrhosis matters as much as the tumor.

SiteWhat really decides treatment
EsophagusT1a vs deeper; node-positive; SCC vs adeno; location; fitness for esophagectomy
StomachT2+ or N+ (perioperative chemo); peritoneal disease on laparoscopy
PancreasResectability (vessel contact), not TNM number
Liver (HCC)Tumor burden + liver function (Child-Pugh) + performance status (BCLC)
RectumMRI features: T3/T4, MRF, EMVI, nodes, height; MMR status
AnusSize (T) and node location; HIV status

The Core Workup

Before the site-specific details, almost every GI cancer gets the same backbone:

  1. History and exam: weight loss, nutrition, performance status. For anal and low rectal cancer, add DRE, anoscopy, and groin node exam.
  2. Tissue + scope: endoscopy with biopsy (EGD, colonoscopy, or EUS-guided for pancreas). Get a full colonoscopy in rectal cancer to find synchronous lesions.
  3. Local imaging (site-specific; see each site) plus CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for distant disease. PET/CT for esophagus and anus.
  4. Labs and markers: CBC, liver/renal function; CEA (colorectal), CA 19-9 (pancreas), AFP (HCC), HIV (anal).
  5. Biomarkers: MMR/MSI on colorectal, gastric, esophageal, and pancreatic tumors; HER2 and PD-L1 for esophagogastric adenocarcinoma; germline testing for pancreatic cancer.
  6. Supportive: nutrition (feeding tube for obstructing esophageal tumors), smoking cessation, stoma counseling.

Esophagus

How it's staged: AJCC TNM (8th ed.). SCC and adenocarcinoma share the T/N/M definitions but have separate stage groups; for SCC, grade and tumor location also feed the stage group.

Workup adds: EGD + biopsy; EUS for depth and regional/celiac nodes (best T and N tool); CT chest/abdomen and FDG-PET/CT; bronchoscopy if at or above the carina; assign a Siewert category for esophagogastric junction (EGJ) tumors.

Build It Up (T = Depth)

TDepth
T1aMucosa (lamina propria / muscularis mucosae)
T1bSubmucosa
T2Muscularis propria
T3Adventitia
T4aResectable neighbors (pleura, pericardium, azygos, diaphragm, peritoneum)
T4bUnresectable (aorta, vertebral body, airway)

Nodes by count: N1 = 1–2, N2 = 3–6, N3 = ≥7. Celiac nodes are regional; supraclavicular nodes are M1.

The Practical Treatment Split

  • T1a → endoscopic resection (EMR + ablation)
  • T1b–T2, N0 → esophagectomy
  • T3–T4a or N+ → neoadjuvant chemoRT then surgery (trimodality) for SCC; perioperative chemo or trimodality for adeno
  • T4b or medically unfit → definitive chemoRT
Traps and high-yield
  • Siewert type III EGJ tumors (epicenter 2–5 cm below the EGJ) are treated as gastric, not esophageal.
  • Cervical esophageal tumors (<5 cm from the cricopharyngeus) → definitive chemoRT, not surgery.
  • If histology is unknown, it defaults to the SCC staging system.

Stomach

How it's staged: AJCC TNM, with the same depth logic as the colon and the same nodal count as the esophagus.

Workup adds: EGD + biopsy; EUS (preferred when early-stage disease is suspected); CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; FDG-PET/CT for locally advanced disease; H. pylori testing; diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal washings for clinical T1b or higher being considered for resection.

Build It Up (T = Depth)

TDepth
T1aLamina propria / muscularis mucosae
T1bSubmucosa
T2Muscularis propria
T3Subserosa
T4aSerosa (visceral peritoneum)
T4bAdjacent organs

Nodes by count: N1 = 1–2, N2 = 3–6, N3 = ≥7 (same as esophagus).

What drives treatment: T2+ or N+ disease → perioperative chemotherapy around gastrectomy (consider perioperative immunotherapy if MSI-H/dMMR).

Traps and high-yield
  • Positive peritoneal cytology = M1 (stage IV) even with no visible implants. This is why laparoscopy with washings matters before committing to curative surgery.
  • Occult peritoneal disease is found in a meaningful fraction of CT-negative patients, especially with linitis plastica.

Pancreas: Resectability Is the Stage That Matters

How it's staged: TNM exists for prognosis (T by size: ≤2, >2–4, >4 cm; T4 = arterial involvement; N1 = 1–3 nodes, N2 = ≥4), but treatment decisions are made on resectability from a pancreatic-protocol (dual-phase, thin-slice) CT, decided by multidisciplinary consensus.

Workup adds: dedicated pancreatic CT (preferred) or MRI with contrast, done before stenting when possible; EUS-guided biopsy; CA 19-9 (interpret after bilirubin normalizes); germline testing.

The Categories (Artery vs Vein Contact)

CategoryArteries (SMA, celiac, CHA)Veins (SMV, portal vein)
ResectableNo arterial contactNo contact, or ≤180° without contour irregularity
BorderlineSMA ≤180°; CHA contact that's reconstructable; CA ≤180° (body/tail)>180°, or ≤180° with contour irregularity/thrombosis, but reconstructable
Locally advancedSMA or CA >180° (any location)Unreconstructable (complete occlusion)

Treatment Logic

  • Resectable → surgery (Whipple for head/uncinate; distal pancreatectomy + splenectomy for body/tail) → adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX. Neoadjuvant chemo is increasingly used.
  • Borderline / locally advanced → neoadjuvant therapy, then reassess for resection based on response.
Quick check: head tumor, SMV contact 200° with a short, reconstructable segment, no arterial contact. Category?▾

Borderline resectable. Venous contact >180° that can be reconstructed. Plan: neoadjuvant chemo (± RT), then surgery with vein resection.

Traps and high-yield
  • Any distant metastasis, including non-regional nodes, makes it unresectable regardless of vessel anatomy.
  • Locally advanced ≠ permanently unresectable: a good response to neoadjuvant therapy can convert some to resectable.
  • Extension into the transverse colon, stomach, spleen, adrenal, or kidney is not an automatic contraindication: those organs can come out with the specimen.

Liver (HCC): Stage by BCLC, Not TNM

How it's staged: the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system, because you must weigh the tumor and the underlying liver. It combines tumor burden + liver function (Child-Pugh) + performance status and maps each stage directly to a treatment.

Workup adds: multiphase CT or contrast-enhanced MRI; AFP; hepatitis panel; assessment of liver reserve and portal hypertension (varices, splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia); noncontrast chest CT for lung mets. FDG-PET is not recommended for HCC staging (low sensitivity).

The Stages (Burden → Function → PS)

BCLCTumor / function / PSTreatment
0 (very early)Single ≤2 cm, preserved function, PS 0Resection / ablation / transplant
A (early)Single, or ≤3 nodules each ≤3 cm; preserved function, PS 0Resection / ablation / transplant
B (intermediate)Multinodular, preserved function, PS 0TACE
C (advanced)Portal invasion and/or extrahepatic spread, PS 1–2Systemic therapy
D (terminal)Any burden, end-stage liver function, PS 3–4Best supportive care

Child-Pugh uses bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, and encephalopathy (Class A compensated; B/C decompensated). Most systemic agents are studied in Child-Pugh A.

Where radiation fits: SBRT and Y-90 serve as bridging to transplant, for tumors not suited to ablation, and for portal vein tumor thrombus. Liver SBRT is generally reserved for Child-Pugh A or B7.

Traps and high-yield
  • A large solitary HCC (>5 cm) without vascular invasion may still be resected, even though size alone could suggest intermediate stage.
  • TNM is mainly used for pathologic staging after transplant; it does not drive pretreatment decisions.

Rectum: Stage on MRI

How it's staged: AJCC TNM, but the clinically decisive staging tool is high-resolution pelvic MRI, which defines both T/N and the risk features that select neoadjuvant therapy.

Workup adds: full colonoscopy with biopsy; rectal-protocol MRI; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; CEA; MMR/MSI status.

Build It Up (T = Depth)

TDepth
T1Submucosa
T2Muscularis propria
T3Into mesorectal fat (a <1 mm, b 1–5 mm, c 5–15 mm, d >15 mm)
T4aThrough peritoneum
T4bInvades other organs

Nodes by count: N1a = 1, N1b = 2–3, N1c = tumor deposits only, N2a = 4–6, N2b = ≥7.

The MRI Risk Features That Push Toward TNT

  • cT4a/T4b
  • Threatened or involved MRF (CRM ≤1 mm)
  • EMVI positive
  • cN2 / enlarged lateral pelvic nodes
  • Low tumors where organ preservation is the goal
Biology overrides anatomy: MMR-deficient tumors (~5–10%) change the plan. Immunotherapy first.

Treatment Logic

  • Low-risk (e.g., T1–2 N0, clear MRF) → upfront surgery; selected early T1 can have local excision.
  • Locally advanced (T3 N any, T1–2 N1–2, T4) → neoadjuvant therapy then TME: short-course RT (25 Gy/5), long-course chemoRT (50.4 Gy/28 + capecitabine), or TNT. For mid/upper tumors with a clear MRF, FOLFOX with selective RT (PROSPECT) is an option.
Quick check: mid-rectal T2N0, MRF clear, MMR-proficient. Does this patient need radiation?▾

Not routinely. Early rectal cancer goes straight to TME. Neoadjuvant therapy is considered only for organ preservation in a low tumor.

Traps and high-yield
  • EMVI and tumor deposits outperform nodal status for predicting distant recurrence: don't anchor only on N.
  • The RAPIDO 5-year update showed higher locoregional recurrence with short-course RT in high-risk disease, so short-course is chosen cautiously there.
  • A complete clinical response may qualify selected patients for watch-and-wait at experienced centers.

Anus: Size and Node Location (the Nodal Exception)

How it's staged: AJCC TNM (9th ed.), unique in GI because T is by tumor size (not wall depth) and N is by node location (not count).

Workup adds: DRE + inguinal node exam; anoscopy; chest/abdomen CT + pelvis CT or MRI; consider FDG-PET/CT; HIV testing; gynecologic/cervical screening.

T by Size, N by Location

TSizeNLocation
T1≤2 cmN1aInguinal, mesorectal, superior rectal, internal iliac, or obturator
T2>2–5 cmN1bExternal iliac
T3>5 cmN1cExternal iliac + any N1a
T4Invades adjacent organ (vagina, urethra, bladder)

Treatment logic: nearly all anal canal SCC is treated with definitive chemoRT (5-FU/mitomycin + RT), including T1N0, not surgery. Surgery is reserved for small anal-margin lesions or salvage.

Traps and high-yield
  • The 9th-edition change: node positivity now starts at stage IIB (T1–2 N1), and tumors >5 cm became stage IIIA, because T category outweighs N for survival in anal cancer.
  • Treatment doesn't change based on HIV status alone.

NCCN Workup by Site

What the NCCN Esophageal/Gastric, Pancreatic, Hepatobiliary, Rectal, and Anal Carcinoma Guidelines recommend before treatment, simplified for learning. Always check the current guideline for real patients.

DiagnosisEGD + biopsy; EUS if no metastases
ImagingCT chest/abdomen with contrast; PET/CT
BiomarkersHER2 (adenocarcinoma), MMR/MSI, PD-L1
OtherBronchoscopy for tumors at/above the carina; nutrition assessment (feeding tube); surgical evaluation
DiagnosisEGD + biopsy; EUS
ImagingCT chest/abdomen/pelvis; PET/CT if no metastases
Staging surgeryLaparoscopy with peritoneal washings (T1b or higher, before resection)
BiomarkersHER2, MMR/MSI, PD-L1; H. pylori testing
ImagingPancreatic-protocol CT (or MRI), CT chest; ideally before stenting
TissueEUS-guided biopsy (needed before neoadjuvant therapy)
LabsCA 19-9 (after bilirubin normalizes), LFTs
GeneticsGermline testing for everyone; tumor molecular profiling for advanced disease
DecisionMultidisciplinary review of resectability
ImagingMultiphase CT or MRI (LI-RADS); CT chest
LabsAFP, hepatitis B/C, LFTs, INR (Child-Pugh / MELD)
BiopsyNot needed for LI-RADS 5 in cirrhosis; otherwise biopsy
DecisionTransplant / surgery / ablation / liver-directed therapy / systemic, by multidisciplinary team

High-Yield Summary
  • Across most GI sites, T stage is depth through the wall, N stage is the number of involved nodes, and M is distant spread, but anal cancer uses tumor size for T and node location for N.
  • Pancreatic cancer is treated by resectability, based on how much the tumor touches the SMA, celiac axis, hepatic artery, and SMV/portal vein on pancreatic-protocol CT.
  • HCC is staged with BCLC, which combines tumor burden, liver function (Child-Pugh), and performance status and points to a treatment.
  • Positive peritoneal cytology is M1 in stomach cancer, which is why laparoscopy with washings comes before curative surgery.
  • Rectal cancer with T4 disease, a threatened mesorectal fascia, EMVI, N2, or lateral nodes is high risk and gets total neoadjuvant therapy, and dMMR tumors get immunotherapy first.

Treatment Paradigms.title: GI Cancer Treatment Paradigms
Treatment Paradigms.html:
GI treatment differs by organ, but it always comes down to where radiation sits relative to surgery. Ask three questions:

1
Is surgery the cure?

Anus: no, chemoRT is (surgery is salvage). Rectum, esophagus, stomach, pancreas: surgery is central, and RT/chemo are given around it.

2
Early or locally advanced?

Early (T1–2 N0) → surgery or endoscopic resection alone. Locally advanced (T3–4 or N+) → neoadjuvant chemo ± RT.

3
Can the patient have surgery?

If not, definitive chemoRT (esophagus, rectum), SBRT (liver, pancreas), or palliation.

The Big Picture by Site

The Framework

The GI treatment framework

Find your patient's row.

1
If it's…
Anal squamous cell carcinoma (any T, any N, M0)
Definitive chemoRT: IMRT 50.4–54 Gy + 5-FU/capecitabine + mitomycin. APR only for persistent/recurrent disease.
2
If it's…
Early (T1–T2 N0) rectal, esophageal, or gastric cancer
Surgery (or endoscopic resection for T1a), usually no radiation.
3
If it's…
Locally advanced rectal or esophageal cancer (T3–4 or N+)
Neoadjuvant chemoRT (± chemo) → surgery; rectal complete responders can try watch-and-wait.
4
If the patient is…
Not a surgical candidate, or has cervical/SCC esophageal cancer
Definitive chemoRT (esophagus 50.4 Gy) or SBRT (liver, pancreas).
5
If there is…

Anus: chemoRT cures, surgery salvages. Everywhere else: surgery cures, chemoRT prepares.

Paradigm 1: Anal Cancer: Chemoradiation Cures

1
IMRT + 5-FU/cape + mitomycin
→
2
Assess response up to 26 weeks
→
3
Persistent/progressing → biopsy → salvage APR
  • Nigro showed chemoRT could replace APR. RTOG 9811: mitomycin beat cisplatin induction. ACT II: cisplatin no better than mitomycin; maintenance chemo didn't help; many responses complete only by 26 weeks.
  • Every patient gets the groins and pelvic nodes treated. Don't take a break: treatment breaks lower cure.
  • Side effects: severe perineal/groin skin reaction, diarrhea, low counts (mitomycin), later fibrosis, sexual dysfunction, infertility, pelvic fractures.
  • Very small T1N0 anal margin tumors: local excision is an option. HIV patients with good CD4 counts get standard therapy.
Node-negative
T2N0 example

Primary 50.4 Gy/28, elective nodes 42 Gy/28.

Node-positive or T3–4
Dose-painted

Primary 54 Gy/30; involved nodes 50.4 (≤3 cm) or 54 Gy (>3 cm); elective nodes 45 Gy.

Paradigm 2: Early Rectal Cancer (T1–T2 N0)

  • TME surgery (low anterior resection; APR if the sphincter can't be saved). No radiation needed.
  • Small, favorable T1: transanal local excision.
  • Low tumor, patient wants to avoid a stoma: chemoRT/TNT with a goal of organ preservation in selected patients.
  • Pathology upstaged after surgery (pT3 or N+) without neoadjuvant therapy: adjuvant chemo ± chemoRT.

Paradigm 3: Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer (T3–4 or N+)

1
RT (25/5 or 50.4/28 + cape)
↔
2
~4 months FOLFOX/CAPOX (before or after RT)
→
3
Restage: MRI + endoscopy
→
4
TME, or watch-and-wait if cCR
  • Preop beats postop: the German CAO/ARO/AIO-94 trial cut local recurrence (6% vs 13%) with less toxicity.
  • Total neoadjuvant therapy moves all chemo before surgery: RAPIDO (short-course RT then chemo) cut disease-related treatment failure; PRODIGE 23 (chemo then chemoRT) improved survival.
  • Organ preservation: in OPRA, about half of patients kept their rectum with watch-and-wait after TNT (chemoRT then consolidation chemo did best).
  • Selective RT omission: PROSPECT showed FOLFOX with chemoRT only for poor responders was noninferior for mid/upper tumors with a clear MRF.
  • MMR-deficient: dostarlimab alone produced complete responses in essentially all patients (Cercek).
  • Target: tumor + entire mesorectum + presacral, internal iliac, obturator nodes (+ external iliac for T4 anterior organs, + inguinal if the anal canal is involved). Prone or supine with a full bladder.
Node-negative T3, MRF clear
Lower risk

Short- or long-course RT then TME; or FOLFOX with selective RT (PROSPECT).

Node-positive / high risk
TNT

Short-course or long-course RT plus ~4 months of chemo, then TME or watch-and-wait. Long-course for a threatened MRF or T4.

Paradigm 4: Esophageal Cancer

SituationTreatment
T1a (and select T1b)Endoscopic resection (EMR/ESD) ± ablation of Barrett's
T1b–T2 N0, low riskEsophagectomy
T2 N+ / T3–T4a, operable, SCCCROSS chemoRT (41.4 Gy) → esophagectomy, or definitive chemoRT with surgery for residual disease
Same, adenocarcinomaPerioperative FLOT (ESOPEC: better survival than CROSS) or CROSS → esophagectomy
Residual disease after CROSS + surgeryAdjuvant nivolumab for 1 year (CheckMate 577)
Cervical, T4b, or unfitDefinitive chemoRT 50–50.4 Gy (RTOG 8501; 64.8 Gy no better, RTOG 9405)
  • SCC is more radiosensitive: pCR after CROSS ~49% (vs ~23% for adeno), so definitive chemoRT is a real option for SCC.
  • OARs: lungs (V20 <20% before surgery: pulmonary complications), heart (keep mean low), cord, liver, kidneys (distal).
  • Palliative: stent, brachytherapy, or short EBRT for dysphagia/bleeding.

Paradigm 5: Stomach

  • Perioperative FLOT (FLOT4) + gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy is the standard for T2+ or N+.
  • Adjuvant chemoRT (45 Gy) after an inadequate lymph node dissection (INT-0116 / Macdonald) or positive margin. After periop chemo and D2 surgery, adding postop chemoRT didn't help (CRITICS; ARTIST).
  • Palliative RT is very effective for bleeding (e.g., 8 Gy × 1 to 30 Gy/10).

Paradigm 6: Pancreas

Resectable
Surgery-first

Whipple (head) or distal pancreatectomy → adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX (PRODIGE 24: median OS ~54 vs 35 months). Neoadjuvant chemo increasingly used.

Borderline
Neoadjuvant

Chemo (mFOLFIRINOX) ± chemoRT or SBRT → restage → surgery. PREOPANC supported neoadjuvant chemoRT; the role of adding RT to modern chemo is still debated.

Locally advanced
Chemo first

Chemo → chemoRT or SBRT for local control/pain (LAP07: better local control, not survival). Celiac plexus RT for pain.

  • SBRT limit: the duodenum, stomach, and bowel right next to the pancreas (bleeding, ulcer, perforation).

Paradigm 7: Liver (HCC)

  • Curative first choices: transplant (Milan criteria), resection, ablation (≤3 cm).
  • SBRT for tumors not suited to ablation, bridging to transplant, and portal vein thrombus. RTOG 1112: SBRT + sorafenib improved survival vs sorafenib alone.
  • Other liver-directed options: TACE, Y-90 radioembolization. Advanced: atezolizumab + bevacizumab or other systemic therapy.
  • Protect liver function: ≥700 cc of normal liver <15 Gy (SBRT); mean liver dose limits for conventional RT (~28 Gy for primary liver cancer). Child-Pugh A–B7 patients only. Watch for radiation-induced liver disease.

Paradigm 8: Metastatic and Palliative

  • Bleeding (gastric, rectal): short-course RT (8 Gy × 1–2 up to 30 Gy/10).
  • Obstruction/dysphagia: esophageal stent or RT; rectal stent, diversion, or RT.
  • Pain: pancreatic celiac plexus RT; liver capsule pain.
  • Oligometastases (e.g., colorectal liver or lung mets): SBRT when surgery or ablation isn't possible.

Clinical Pearls: The Evidence Behind the Paradigms

Nigro, RTOG 9811, ACT II

Result
5-FU + mitomycin with RT; cisplatin not better; judge response at 26 weeks.
Why it matters

German CAO/ARO/AIO-94

RAPIDO & PRODIGE 23

Result
Fewer treatment failures (RAPIDO) and better survival (PRODIGE 23).
Why it matters
TNT for high-risk rectal cancer.
OPRA
Question
Can TNT allow organ preservation?
Result
~Half kept their rectum with watch-and-wait.
Why it matters
Non-operative management.
CROSS
Question
Preop chemoRT before esophagectomy?
Result
41.4 Gy + carbo/paclitaxel nearly doubled median survival; pCR 29% (49% SCC).
Why it matters
Trimodality standard.
RTOG 8501 & 9405

Definitive treatment for esophageal cancer?
Result
ChemoRT beat RT alone; 64.8 Gy no better than 50.4 Gy.
Why it matters
Definitive dose 50–50.4 Gy.
PRODIGE 24 & LAP07
Question
Adjuvant chemo and RT in pancreatic cancer?
Result
mFOLFIRINOX improved survival after resection; chemoRT for locally advanced improved local control, not survival.
Why it matters
Chemo leads; RT selected.
RTOG 1112
Question
SBRT for unresectable HCC?
Result
SBRT + sorafenib improved overall and progression-free survival.
Why it matters
SBRT is a real HCC option.

High-Yield Summary
  • Anal cancer gets definitive chemoradiation with 5-FU (or capecitabine) and mitomycin, always including the groins, with surgery saved for salvage.
  • Locally advanced rectal cancer gets total neoadjuvant therapy (short-course or long-course RT plus chemo), then TME surgery or watch-and-wait after a complete response, and dMMR tumors get immunotherapy.
  • Locally advanced esophageal cancer gets chemoradiation to 41.4 Gy followed by surgery (CROSS), or definitive chemoradiation to 50 to 50.4 Gy for squamous cancers or unfit patients.
  • Pancreatic cancer treatment is driven by chemo, with RT used selectively for borderline resectable or locally advanced disease.
  • Liver SBRT is an option for HCC that can't be resected or ablated, in patients with good liver function (Child-Pugh A to B7).
